thread.title: UPDATE: How your iPhone could save your life

author: morningstar.com
title: UPDATE: How your iPhone could save your life
text:
By Quentin Fottrell, MarketWatch
These apps provide a timely reminder to look after yourself and others
Could an app mean the difference between life and death? Perhaps.
Americans spend more time than ever (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/people-are-spending-most-of-their-waking-hours-staring-at-screens-2018-08-01) swiping their lives away on their tablets and smartphones. That may not be good for psychologists and teachers who are concerned about smartphone addiction and what it's doing to people's ability to concentrate (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/want-to-check-your-phone-or-tablet-during-class-it-may-cost-you-dearly-2018-07-30) at work and school.
But people are willing to spend on iPhones, even those that cost $1,000, and they're willing to pay for apps that make their lives more convenient. That's just part of the reason why Apple stock cleared the $200 mark on Wednesday after the reporting better-than-expected (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/people-are-spending-most-of-their-waking-hours-staring-at-screens-2018-08-01) fiscal third-quarter results.
Having an iPhone nearby can be beneficial to your safety. In 2015, the Find My iPhone app was instrumental in locating a missing Georgia aerospace engineering student. The student, then 24, left a party with his girlfriend's iPhone in his jacket. His friends used the app to locate him.
He was found lying by a train check, suffering from severe dehydration, with broken bones and a punctured lung. One source told local news station CBS46 (http://www.cbs46.com/story/30368114/source-georgia-tech-student-jumped-onto-moving-train) that the teenager had tried to jump onto a moving train from a bridge just like James Bond in the opening scene of "Skyfall." (http://www.cbs46.com/story/30978013/georgia-tech-student-who-allegedly-jumped-onto-train-will-not-be-charged)
Apps are not all fun and games. Many people in the path of Hurricanes Irma and Harvey last year were glued to the TV screens, while others may have downloaded storm-tracking apps for help (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/5-apps-for-tracking-hurricane-joaquin-2015-10-01). They include Hurricane (https://itunes.apple.com/us/app/hurricane-track-for-ios/id437519442?mt=8) (free on iOS and Android) and Hurricane Track (https://itunes.apple.com/us/app/hurricane-track-for-ios/id437519442?mt=8) (free on Apple's(AAPL) iOS).
Several apps use data from the federal National Hurricane Center and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. Apps offer one advantage over tracking the storm online or via television: If the power goes out, they give updates as long as a user's smartphone battery has juice.
(http://www.marketwatch.com/story/new-apple-iphones-key-feature-is-its-price-tag-2017-09-09)Here are five apps that could save your life:
Apps that help people at risk of suicide
Given that the rate of suicide among Americans has spiked over the last 15 years (https://www.cdc.gov/violenceprevention/suicide/index.html), it's probably no surprise that smartphones provide a gateway to help those most at risk. Among the free apps on iOS and Android: A Friend Asks (http://jasonfoundation.com/get-involved/student/a-friend-asks-app/) by the nonprofit Jason Foundation outlines warning signs for young people, including bullying at school, sudden deterioration in school performance and taking unnecessary risks. MY3 (http://my3app.org/) is designed for users who know they have suicidal thoughts. The app gives users three contacts to alert when they feel at risk. They could be a neighbor, a family member or friend or even a therapist. Designed as a "safety tool box," it also has sections to list warning signs and coping strategies.
See also:The surge in the number of teenage suicide attempts (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/the-number-of-children-with-thoughts-of-suicide-and-self-harm-doubled-in-10-years-2017-05-06)
'Do not disturb' stops texting while driving
Apple's iOS 11 operating system includes a do-not-disturb-while-driving feature, which is designed to encourage people to silence their phone without turning it off completely while they drive. Other apps, including Call Bliss (http://nvariance.com/bliss-overviewbenefits/), silence incoming calls and texts while you're driving, while allowing specific people like a child or spouse on an "always allowed" list. Unlike Apple's own free feature, however, Call Bliss costs $9.99. Federal law prohibits train engineers from using cell phones, but there's no federal ban on car drivers. Some 15 states and the District of Columbia, however, do have bans on handheld cellphone use while driving -- including New York, New Jersey and California -- and 47 states and Washington, D.C., explicitly ban texting.
Read also: Move over, breathalyzers; 'textalyzers' could be next (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/move-over-breathalyzers-textalyzers-could-be-used-on-drivers-phones-2017-07-26)
(http://www.marketwatch.com/story/move-over-breathalyzers-textalyzers-could-be-used-on-drivers-phones-2017-07-26)
First-aid help from the American Red Cross
The American Red Cross (http://www.redcross.org/get-help/how-to-prepare-for-emergencies/) mobile-apps has released a series of free apps in recent years on both Android and iOS, including "Hero Care," connecting users to resources to help them in emergencies, "First Aid," giving tips on how to treat people who have severe allergies, choking, bleeding, broken bones or burns, and "Blood Donor," which schedules and tracks blood-donation appointments. Accidents or unintentional injuries are the No. 4 cause of death in the U.S. (42.6 per 100,000 people), according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Apple also has a feature that reminds people to go to bed early to get enough sleep, helpful given that workers with sleep problems were nearly twice as likely to die in a work-related accident, this Swedish study (https://www.nap.edu/read/11617/chapter/6#150) found.
Don't miss:This is the worst mistake people make at work (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/this-is-the-worst-mistake-people-make-at-work-2017-07-26)
Tracking heart rate, blood pressure and workouts
HealthLine.com recently reviewed 10 apps that track heart rate and blood pressure and, in the case of PulsePoint (https://itunes.apple.com/us/app/pulsepoint/id500772134?mt=8) (free on both iOS and Android), even contact emergency services. It uses location-based technology to link to emergency services when someone is having a medical emergency. It describes itself as a "virtual window" into 911-communication centers. It's not available in all areas. iCardio (https://itunes.apple.com/us/app/icardio-workout-tracker-heart-rate-trainer/id314841648?mt=8) (free on iOS and Android) aims to help people work out without overdoing it and keeps track of all your workouts and SmartBP (https://itunes.apple.com/us/app/blood-pressure-smart-blood-pressure-smartbp-bp-tracker/id519076558?mt=8) (also free on iOS and Android) simply allows you to store and track your blood-pressure information. The iOS Health App (https://www.apple.com/ios/health/) also encourages users to keep track of their exercise, sleep, mindfulness and nutrition, and asks people to become organ donors.
See also:The 7 best fitness apps for people over 50 (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/the-7-best-fitness-apps-for-people-over-50-2017-09-06)
Apps that aim to prevent 'hot car' deaths
There are a raft of apps, including Baby on Board (https://www.kars4kids.org/safety-app/) ($1.99) for Android, which simply ask if you've brought your kids, and others designed to prevent infant car deaths. Some of these apps, however, have been labeled as unreliable by some reviewers (https://itunes.apple.com/us/app/precious-cargo-dont-forget-baby-kids-in-car/id1021331965?mt=8). Most simply remind parents when they walk away from the car that there's a child onboard. Sense-A-Life (http://www.sensealife.com/) costs $99 for a car seat and access to a mobile app. When the guardian or parent walks away from the car seat, it sends an alert if the child is still in it. It also tracks the location of the car and a sensor that requires two pounds of pressure on a child seat to activate the device. Failing that, Walmart (WMT) sells a SensorSafe (http://bit.ly/2w1h2GO) car seat ($150) that sounds an alarm to remind parents that a baby is on board.
Tracking the eye of the storm with your iPhone
Many people in the path of Hurricanes Irma and Harvey last year were glued to the TV screens, while others may have downloaded storm-tracking apps for help (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/5-apps-for-tracking-hurricane-joaquin-2015-10-01). There's no single official government hurricane app, but several products on the market use data from the federal National Hurricane Center and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. Apps offer one advantage over tracking the storm online or via television: If the power goes out, they'll continue to give updates as long as a user's smartphone battery has juice. They include Hurricane (https://itunes.apple.com/us/app/hurricane-track-for-ios/id437519442?mt=8) (free on iOS and Android) and Hurricane Track (https://itunes.apple.com/us/app/hurricane-track-for-ios/id437519442?mt=8) (free on Apple's(AAPL) iOS).
-Quentin Fottrell; 415-439-6400; AskNewswires@dowjones.com
